title: A NUL byte splits one value into two: the C login check truncates, the scripting layer keeps the tail
index_line: T-0043 · EXEC · embedded NUL authenticates as the short name but is persisted whole into a Lua session file · c/lua · corroborated
invariant_violated: A string crossing a C/scripting boundary is assumed to mean the same thing on both sides. It does not: the C path measures with a NUL-terminated view, the scripting layer carries an explicit length. A value with an embedded NUL is therefore *two different values* depending on who looks — and the half the C code never saw is the half the script persists.

mechanism.does: the attacker logs in with a username containing a NUL byte followed by script source
the C authentication path sees the NUL-terminated prefix, so it checks — and accepts — the short, valid name
the request handler hands the same bytes to the scripting layer, which carries an explicit length and keeps the tail
the session record is serialised by the scripting layer, so the tail is written as statements rather than data
the session file is loaded as a script on the next request and the injected statements execute
the injected code runs a command as the service account (root or SYSTEM in the default install)

source.http.request.value: the login form field — an embedded NUL is the whole payload; filters that treat the value as text never see past it

sink.eval.value: the scripting engine loading the session record back as source (Lua `loadfile`, PHP `include` of a cache, Python `exec` of a pickle-adjacent cache)

encoding.string.value: the NUL itself; the split is between the C string view and the length-carrying view

guard.escaping.value: there is no escaping step between the caller's string and the persisted record — the 'guard' is the implicit assumption that both layers agree on length

preconditions.expr: the service embeds a scripting engine and persists per-user state as code it later loads

check.spec: find / -name '*.lua' -o -name 'sessions' -type d 2>/dev/null | head; ldd $(command -v the-service) 2>/dev/null | grep -i lua

preconditions.expr: a login field accepts a NUL byte without rejecting the request

spec.method: read the service version banner or the binary's version string and compare with the vendor's fixed release

success: a username with an embedded NUL authenticates as the prefix, and the session file on disk contains the tail as statements
the injected code runs on the *next* request, when the session is reloaded
the effect is pre-authentication even though it looks like a post-auth session write
failure_like: the field is length-checked or the scripting layer re-validates the persisted record before loading it
session state is stored as data (JSON/DB rows) rather than executable source
false_positive: a login that fails with the NUL payload — the truncation check is the first half; without the persist-and-load half there is no bug
a session file containing the NUL because it was written as escaped data — check whether the file is loaded as code

hazards: any C↔script boundary is a candidate: Lua/PHP/Python embedded in a C daemon, with session or cache files written as source
the NUL is usually rejected by the web framework but not by the socket read — test the raw request, not a form submission
the two halves must both exist: truncation alone is a filter bypass; persistence-as-code alone is a design smell. Record only when they compose
related to T-0019 (record injection into a flat store) but the mechanism is a length-view mismatch inside one value, not a delimiter
non_transfers: languages whose strings carry explicit lengths on both sides of the boundary (no truncation)
session stores that are data, not source

provenance.author: RCE Security (Julien Ahrens) analysis of CVE-2025-47812
provenance.corroborates: the strlen-vs-NUL behaviour in the login handler, the Lua session file as the persistence point, and the pre-auth RCE chain

provenance.author: Huntress (independent, in-the-wild)
provenance.corroborates: independent exploitation reporting and detection guidance
